title: Bukit Sembawang Estates wins Top Selling Landed Project for third year running, with Pollen Collection II
article:
Homes at Pollen Collection II, Bukit Sembawang Estates’ 186-unit development in the Seletar Hills landed enclave, were quietly released for sale last December, with an initial 52 units launched.

Since then, the developer has released more residences. As at Sept 30, 110 homes at Pollen Collection II have been launched, based on project details on URA’s Realis database.

Caveats lodged as at Oct 27 show that 52 units have been sold, with prices averaging around $2,500 psf. That works out to 47% of the homes released to date.

The largest transaction by absolute value was for a corner terraced house occupying a 2,540 sq ft plot, which fetched 5.78million(2,276 psf) in April.

The sales at Pollen Collection II garnered it the Top Selling Landed Project title at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026. The award is given to new landed housing projects that record the highest number of sales across a designated 12-month period.

This is the third consecutive time that Bukit Sembawang Estates has scooped up the award. In the past two editions of the EPEA, the developer won the Top Selling Landed Project title for Pollen Collection.

Latest Nim Collection phase

Pollen Collection II is part of Nim Collection, Bukit Sembawang Estates’ master-planned landed precinct on Nim Road, off Ang Mo Kio Avenue 5. The developer has gradually activated the site, launching it in four phases thus far.

Nim Collection Phase 1 and Nim Collection Phase 2 were launched in 2018. They comprise 98 fully sold terraced houses, with 99-year leasehold tenures, that were completed in 2019.

In October 2022, the developer launched the third phase, Pollen Collection. The 99-year leasehold project, made up of 128 terraced houses and two pairs of semi-detached homes, was progressively released for sale over two years.

Caveats lodged show the project is 94% sold, with only eight units remaining. Homes taken up fetched an average land rate of around $2,160 psf. The project was completed earlier this year.

Pollen Collection II is the fourth phase and latest addition to the enclave. The 99-year leasehold development, sited between Nim Collection and Pollen Collection, consists of 186 terraced homes.

There is one remaining plot in the Nim Road precinct that is slated to become the fifth phase in the enclave. Spanning 205,528 sq ft, the freehold site can accommodate 85 houses, per the Written Permission granted by URA in April 2025.

Masterful design

Like the earlier collections, Pollen Collection II was designed by acclaimed Singapore firm W Architects.

The terraced homes include 160 intermediate units occupying land areas of between 1,615 and 1,733 sq ft, with floor areas ranging from 4,457 to 4,589 sq ft. There are also 26 corner units, which span larger plots of between 2,287 and 3,470 sq ft, with floor areas ranging from 4,592 to 5,316 sq ft.

Homes at Pollen Collection II were designed to offer the best of landed living, with spacious interiors, private outdoor spaces, and amenities that future-proof the home. All units consist of five levels, including a mezzanine and an attic.

At the first level are the main living spaces. The open-plan layout features living and dining areas with a 5.7m double-volume ceiling, providing expansive, airy spaces at which to gather and entertain. Wet and dry kitchens are provided, along with a household shelter and service yard.

Each home has five bedrooms, each with an en suite bathroom, located on the upper floors. There is also a study next to the master bedroom, which owners can adapt to their needs.

The homes incorporate multiple outdoor spaces, including balconies outside each bedroom, an outdoor garden on the mezzanine level, a courtyard on the third floor, and a rooftop terrace.

In addition to bringing natural light into the home and enhancing cross-ventilation, they provide additional spaces which owners can use for rest, recreation or socialising. For instance, the terrace on the mezzanine floor can be turned into an outdoor lounge or an alfresco dining area, while the courtyard on Level 3 could double as a workout zone.

Larger corner terraced homes feature bigger outdoor spaces, with selected units that come with a swimming pool.

A wheelchair-accessible glass-door electric lift is provided in each home, allowing convenient access to all floors. The car porch, which can hold two vehicles, is fitted with isolator points for two electric-vehicle (EV) chargers.

In addition, the houses integrate solar panels on the roof, enabling owners to harness solar power to offset electricity consumption. Solar energy from the panels will be used to power home features such as the lift and the EV chargers.

With Pollen Collection II’s considered spatial planning and thoughtful design features, Bukit Sembawang Estates continues to set the benchmark for new landed housing projects in Singapore.

Pollen Collection II is expected to be completed in June 2029.

title: Landed living at The Brighton Collection takes on a thoughtful, enduring vision
article:
Intergenerational living has become one of the strongest draws for landed home buyers today, and it is the concept driving The Brighton Collection — a trio of freehold terraced houses in District 19.

Located at 8, 8A and 8B Brighton Crescent, the project by homegrown boutique real estate developer FRX Capital has been named Top Landed Development at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026.

The Brighton Collection comprises two corner terraced homes and one intermediate terraced home within Serangoon Garden, a sought-after landed residential estate known for its tranquillity, strong community appeal, and proximity to the beloved Chomp Chomp Food Centre.

Each unit has two storeys, a basement and an attic, with estimated land sizes ranging from 2,168 to 3,018 sq ft as well as built-up areas of between 5,955 and 7,256 sq ft.

The homes are configured to support multigenerational living, with up to five bedrooms and five en suite bathrooms each.

“Buyers appreciated how the homes maximise every square foot of land without compromising on luxury, comfort or quality. The five-bedroom configuration and generous bedroom sizes were particularly well-received by families who genuinely needed the space,” says a spokesperson for FRX Capital.

“From the high-speed lift to the thoughtfully handpicked fittings, every detail reflects a careful balance between practicality and refined living, creating homes that are functional by design, yet luxurious in experience.”

The developer had acquired the bungalow at 8 Brighton Crescent for $12.4 million last March, before redeveloping it into the three terraced units. FRX Capital launched the trio for sale in October 2025, with asking prices of $6.8 million to $8.3 million.

Tropical modern, by design

DS Architects designed the homes around a tropical modern approach, applying the principle that form follows function, adapted to Singapore’s climate.

Rather than relying on unnecessary complexity, the architecture embraces clarity and purpose, prioritising natural light, ventilation and liveability throughout.

A refined front box frame defines the façade, establishing a strong yet understated presence. Carefully proportioned, the framing element adds structure and definition, avoiding the imposing scale often associated with larger landed homes, while still conveying a sense of modern elegance.

A key feature of the design is the sheltered, generously sized basement carpark. By relocating parking below ground, each home benefits from ample space to comfortably accommodate multiple vehicles.

With the main living spaces elevated above the carpark, the homes enjoy enhanced privacy, improved access to natural light and a more considered spatial hierarchy.

The freed-up ground level further enables seamless integration of lifestyle spaces, with living areas flowing into outdoor decking zones, ideal for family gatherings and entertainment.

In addition, the central courtyard enhances cross-ventilation, keeping the home open and breathable.

Understated and sustainable

Inside, clean lines and a neutral material palette create a calm, timeless backdrop.

“Every home is designed to unlock the full potential of its land, maximising space while creating room for life to unfold. More than architecture, it is a canvas for the owner’s signature — a home that evolves with its residents, gathering character, memories and meaning through the years,” says DS Architects’ director Koh Choon Ngee.

The design of the three Brighton Crescent houses takes a holistic approach to sustainability, integrating architectural strategies, considered material choices and smart-home technologies as part of a more responsible way of living.

This includes the use of recycled and repurposed construction materials, such as building waste incorporated into hardcore layers and certified recycled laminates.

Energy-efficient and smart-enabled systems are also integrated throughout.

The homes are equipped with a premium suite of Fisher & Paykel appliances, incorporating intelligent and safety-driven technologies.

Selected appliances are WiFi-enabled and integrated with the SmartHQ app, allowing residents to monitor, operate and receive notifications remotely.

A visual-audio intercom system, paired with a mobile app, lets residents manage visitor access remotely with greater convenience.

Swift sell-out

In an exclusive early-access event ahead of the official launch, a carefully targeted audience had been introduced to the homes — and their efficient space planning, thoughtful design and concept of multigenerational living.

The campaign appealed to families upgrading from HDB flats and condos, as well as existing landed homeowners seeking a newly rebuilt, more functional and luxurious home without the complexities of reconstruction.

This approach translated into strong early-buyer response, with all three homes sold within months of launch, primarily on the strength of the floor plans and the project’s conceptual positioning.

Going by URA Realis caveat data, the five-bedroom corner terraced house at 8B Brighton Crescent was sold for $7.8 million this January, while the four-bedroom intermediate terraced house at 8A Brighton Crescent was transacted at $6.8 million in April.

The Brighton Collection development is scheduled for completion in the second quarter of 2027.

title: Bidadari Park: An award-winning urban landscape and biophilic sanctuary
article:
Bidadari Park is a vibrant 13ha destination that serves as the ecological spine of the Bidadari public housing estate.

Designed by CPG Consultants with landscape architecture by Henning Larsen, the public park blends ecological conservation, innovative stormwater management and rich heritage within a high-density residential area.

A joint effort by HDB, National Parks Board and national water agency PUB, the project has been recognised for Excellence in Urban Park Landscape at the EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) 2026.

The park seamlessly connects surrounding residential neighbourhoods, commercial and lifestyle amenities, as well as transport infrastructure, forming a cohesive and convenient live-work-play environment.

Residents and visitors can access the park via sheltered walkways and connections from MRT and bus interchanges, a 100m elevated land bridge linking residential estates on higher ground, and a dedicated link bridge from The Woodleigh Mall.

Completed in 2024, the park is bounded by Bidadari Park Drive, Bartley Walk, Upper Aljunied Road and Sang Nila Utama Road.

"Bidadari Park is interesting because it’s next to a [former] cemetery, and the existing site has many resident and migratory birds,” says Ng Sze Oun, director of Compound Collaborative and an EPEA 2026 judge in the Landscape Design specialisation.

“They have taken the opportunity to create a habitat that is more focused on nature than on people,” he adds.

Climate resilience and water-sensitive infrastructure

Bidadari Park serves as a blueprint for climate-focused urban planning, incorporating Singapore’s first multifunctional drainage system within a public park.

At its centre lies the 1.8ha Alkaff Lake, a recreational waterbody that also functions as a stormwater retention pond during heavy rain.

It can hold up to 40,000 cubic metres of water — equivalent to 16 Olympic-sized swimming pools — and regulates stormwater discharge downstream to mitigate flood risks for the estate and surrounding areas.

All of the stormwater in the park is managed on-site through a network of naturalised swales, marshes, wetlands and cascading streams — instead of conventional concrete drains.

Rainwater is filtered through dense vegetation and channelled towards Alkaff Lake, while terraced wetlands help remove sediments, nutrients and pollutants from surface runoff.

Gross pollutant traps installed upstream intercept floating debris, litter and pollutants before stormwater enters the lake system.

An integrated public warning and flood management system also provides timely alerts and evacuation notices when rising water levels are anticipated.

Another engineering feature is Singapore’s first underground service reservoir, concealed beneath a community playfield. It stores treated drinking water for the surrounding township while allowing the space above to be used for recreation.

Woodland sanctuary for biodiversity

Guided by core design principles to protect the existing terrain, the development retained approximately 84% of mature trees on-site, including those on the iconic Rain Tree Island situated within Alkaff Lake.

To enrich the local ecosystem, over 170 species of native plants — totalling roughly 140,000 plants — were added across the park, expanding ecological diversity in the vicinity.

Existing woodlands were also carefully preserved and enhanced with dense native planting to create a continuous shaded canopy that improves air quality, reduces urban heat and further strengthens biodiversity within the estate.

Sustainable construction practices were adopted throughout the development.

Felled trees were repurposed into site furniture and habitat logs, and all horticultural waste was recycled.

Rubble stones salvaged from former cemetery structures were reused as paving materials, while demolished concrete aggregates were also reused in woodland trails.

Designated “no-light zones” in ecologically sensitive woodland areas minimise disturbance to nocturnal wildlife and reduce energy consumption.

Today, Bidadari Park represents one of the last two remaining woodland sanctuaries in Singapore for endangered migratory bird species along the East-Australasian Flyway.

The park supports over 193 species of wildlife, including more than 160 species of resident and migratory birds.

Species such as the Changeable Hawk-Eagle, Brahminy Kite, White-Throated Kingfisher and rare Ruddy Kingfisher have returned to the site, which points to improving ecosystem health and freshwater habitat quality.

Meanwhile, Oriental Pied Hornbills have successfully nested and fledged young within the woodlands.

Connecting communities through nature

Designed to foster active living, the park features over 6km of nature trails and boardwalks, alongside a 2km barrier-free greenway connecting surrounding residential precincts to the park.

Sheltered linkways and other transport connections provide all-weather access across the estate, supporting recreational activities such as walking, jogging and cycling.

One of the park’s most distinct features is the 100m land bridge that links higher-ground residential estates, designed as Singapore’s first eco -pedestrian linkway to accommodate both wildlife and pedestrian movements.

In addition, residents can experience a distinct side of Bidadari by walking along the approximately 300m Heritage Walk — created from the former Upper Aljunied Road and featuring interpretive storyboards celebrating the site’s cultural identity — and visiting the memorial garden with conserved relics and naturalistic planting.

The enhancement of existing woodlands has also encouraged the return of birdwatchers and wildlife enthusiasts.

Shared spaces including bird observation pods, nest shelters and viewing decks bring communities together to discover wildlife, exchange knowledge, and participate in ecological learning programmes.

At Adventure Playwoods, children can move freely among logs, plants and play features integrated into the natural landscape beneath mature rain tree canopies.

Lakefront lawns, picnic areas and cafés provide further opportunities for social interaction.

With its integrated landscape infrastructure and ecological features, Bidadari Park brings residents close to nature and biodiversity, community spaces and leisure amenities, enhancing the liveability of the surrounding residential neighbourhoods.

title: Singapore REITs Are Down: Which 3 Could Recover First?
article:
Investors in Singapore real estate investment trusts (REITs) have had a rough year thus far.
As at 5 November 2026, the
CSOP iEdge S-REIT Leaders Index ETF
(SGX: SRT) is down 11% year-to-date (YTD) against a 13.7% gain for the broader
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI)
So, are
REITs
worth a second look?
Maybe, but a rebound won’t lift them all equally.
The ones with solid balance sheets, dependable rent and an upcoming catalyst should move first.
In this article, we spotlight three REITs that fit that description in different ways, which could stand to benefit once sentiment for the industry turns around.

Ranked by how ready they look for a recovery,

(SGX: C2PU) comes first, followed by
Keppel DC REIT
(SGX: AJBU), then
Sasseur REIT
(SGX: CRPU).
Parkway Life REIT, or PLife REIT – As safe as it gets
PLife REIT owns Singapore hospitals, alongside nursing homes in Japan and France.
Its balance sheet is the strongest here; leverage is low at 33.8%.
Meanwhile, interest is covered over 8.2x with an all-in borrowing cost of just 1.67%, and about 96% of its rate exposure is hedged.
Its weighted average debt maturity will extend to 3.6 years once a maturing loan is refinanced.
The recurring rental income it earns is about as locked in as REIT income gets.
Leases average 14.6 years and most come with built-in annual rental escalations.
These features helped lift DPU 14.6% to S$0.0877 in 1H2026 (ended 30 June 2026), adding to steady growth since its 2007 listing.
Occupancy is 100% in both Singapore and France, while Japan trails at 94.3% after a tenant exited five nursing homes, which weighed on revenue.
Looking forward, the main catalysts for PLife REIT come from continued rent increases across its properties and the potential expansion into more European markets or the UK, which management is studying.
The key risk would be
higher interest rates
, which could increase financing costs and put some downward pressure on unit prices.
Regardless, given the strength of its balance sheet, PLife REIT could be the first to benefit when sentiment turns.
Keppel DC REIT, or KDCREIT – Riding the Data Centre Boom
KDCREIT owns
data centres
in Asia Pacific and Europe, where demand is still running hot.
Its rents show it.
Rental renewals in 9M2026 (ended 30 September 2026) were signed at about 14% higher rates, pushing DPU up 11.7% to S$0.08571.
Occupancy improved slightly to 93.0%.
Cardiff continues to be unoccupied, so a new tenant there would lift income.
Leases average 6.5 years by space, and gearing of 36.2% (38.8% after its latest Tokyo purchase) leaves room for more acquisitions.
The catch is concentration.
Internet companies account for 70.2% of rental income, and the REIT’s single largest tenant alone accounts for more than 40%.
A slowdown in rental growth could also pressure DPU growth moving forward.
Management is also studying power upgrades and redevelopment at older sites, which could add income but would mean more capital spending.
The upside? Continued momentum in rental growth, higher occupancy rates and more accretive acquisitions.
KDCREIT doesn’t really need a sector rally to grow, because rising rents can lift its earnings largely on their own; nevertheless, a sector rally could see KDCREIT be among the first beneficiaries.
Sasseur REIT – Cheap, but There’s a Reason
Sasseur REIT owns four outlet malls in China.
At about S$0.61 as of 4 November 2026, it offers a yield of about 10.7% and trades below its NAV of S$0.82 per unit.
Debt isn’t why it’s cheap.
Gearing sits at just 25.6%, borrowing costs have fallen to a low of 3.7%, and its average debt maturity is decent at 4.8 years, with no refinancing requirement until 2030.
The discount is about China.
Sasseur’s rent comes from an agreement with its outlet operator that combines a fixed amount, rising 3% a year, with a share of sales.
Tenant sales have held up, reaching a record RMB 2.3 billion in 1H2026 (ended 30 June 2026), up 7.4%, and DPU rose 10.2% to S$0.03366.
Leases with the brands inside its malls are short, though, averaging 1.5 years by space.
Its income is also in RMB, so a weaker RMB reduces both its distributions and NAV in Singapore-dollar terms.
A slowdown in Chinese spending would hit both rent and property values, which could mean lower payouts.
A consumer-targeted stimulus by the government and lower rates, on the other hand, could narrow the gap to NAV.
The cheapest of the three, Sasseur has the most potential upside if you’re willing to underwrite the China risk; its 10.7% yield is the incentive for investors.
What Could Delay a REIT Recovery?
A rebound isn’t guaranteed.
If interest rates stay high, refinancing will keep eating into distributions.
Weaker tenant demand or negative rental reversions would hurt income, and more DPU cuts across the sector would keep investors wary.
Lower property values would also push gearing up.
Investors may also keep favouring banks and growth stocks, which have done much better this year.
A steep fall in a REIT’s unit price doesn’t automatically mean a recovery will follow.
Get Smart: Look for the REITs With a Catalyst
A REIT recovery, when it comes, probably won’t be even.
Parkway Life looks the steadiest candidate, while KDCREIT has rental growth on its side, and Sasseur REIT has the most room to rise if its discount narrows.
Rather than buying whatever has fallen furthest, ask what could actually push a REIT’s income and valuation higher.
The ones with a clear answer deserve a closer look.

title: Ahead of OCBC’s 3Q Update: 3 Key Metrics Investors Must Watch
article:
Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation Limited
(SGX: O39), or OCBC, posted a record profit for the first half of 2026.
On the surface, the numbers looked great.
Look a little closer, though, and the source of that profit tells a more interesting story.
With OCBC’s third-quarter business update due on 6 November 2026, now is a good time to take that closer look.
For context, OCBC is Singapore’s longest-established
local bank
.
It was formed in 1932 when three local banks merged.
Today, it is the second-largest financial services group in Southeast Asia by assets, with close to 390 branches and representative offices across 19 countries and regions.
Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and Greater China are its key markets.
In the first half of 2026 (1H2026), OCBC’s total income rose 11% year on year (YoY) to S$8 billion.
Operating profit before allowances grew 12% to S$4.9 billion.
Net profit attributable to shareholders climbed 13% YoY to a record S$4.2 billion.
Shareholders got a slice of the gains, too.
The board declared an interim dividend of S$0.47 per share, up 15% from S$0.41 a year ago.
Here’s the thing: the record didn’t come from OCBC’s lending margins.
It came from fees, trading and insurance.
The big question now is whether that mix can hold.
Which numbers should investors track on 6 November?

Has OCBC’s margin squeeze run its course?
Think of net interest margin (NIM) as the profit margin a bank earns on its loans.
OCBC’s NIM narrowed to 1.73% in 1H2026, down from 1.98% a year ago.
That’s a drop of 0.25 percentage points, and it pulled net interest income (NII) down 3% YoY to S$4.5 billion.
Management isn’t expecting a sharp fall from here.
Its guidance points to only a slight decline in NII for FY2026.
On 6 November, watch whether NIM holds near 1.73% or keeps sliding.
A stable margin would suggest the pressure is easing.
A further drop would put more weight on OCBC’s other income streams.
Can loan growth keep cushioning the blow?
Here, OCBC has a buffer.
Customer loans grew 12% YoY to S$364.5 billion.
That extra volume absorbed most of the margin squeeze.
In other words, NII fell only 3% even though NIM dropped by 0.25 percentage points.
On 7 August 2026, management raised its FY2026 guidance to high-single-digit to low-double-digit loan growth.
OCBC’s 12% pace sits at the top of that range.
On 6 November, check whether growth holds there or slows towards high single digits.
Faster lending only helps if borrowers pay the money back.
For now, asset quality looks steady.
OCBC’s non-performing loan ratio held at 0.9%, unchanged from a year ago.
Investors should make sure it stays there as the loan book grows.
Will fee and wealth income keep carrying the bank?
This is where OCBC earned its record.
Non-interest income rose 36% YoY to S$3.5 billion in 1H2026.
That’s close to 44% of total income.
Fees and commissions climbed 26% YoY to S$1.4 billion as wealth management activity picked up.
Trading income rose 46% to S$1.1 billion.
Income from life and general insurance grew 49% to S$791 million as
Great Eastern Holdings Limited
(SGX: G07) delivered stronger underwriting and investment results.
Not all income is created equal.
Wealth management fees tend to recur because clients keep their assets with the bank.
Trading income is different; it can swing from one quarter to the next with market conditions.
That’s why the split matters on 6 November.
If fees keep growing, OCBC’s diversification looks durable. If trading gains drive most of the increase, it pays to be more cautious.
What has management promised for FY2026?
When it upgraded its guidance in August, management said it expects high-single-digit to low-double-digit loan growth for FY2026.
It also expects total income to grow, with only a slight decline in NII.
This is the yardstick for the third-quarter update.
If management holds or raises its guidance, that would suggest the first-half trends carried into the third quarter.
A downgrade would signal that margins or loan demand weakened faster than the bank expected.
As for
dividends
, don’t expect one on 6 November.
OCBC pays dividends twice a year, so its third-quarter update usually comes without one.
The interim dividend of S$0.47 per share remains the latest signal of the board’s confidence.
Get Smart: Check what fills the gap
A
record profit
makes a great headline.
When a bank’s margin is shrinking, though, the more useful question is what’s filling the gap.
In 1H2026, OCBC’s answer was loan growth and fee income.

title: What’s so wrong with high interest rates?
article:
It could take a while for investors to adjust to
higher interest rates
. After all, it was four years ago in 2022 when central banks embarked on serious monetary tightening.
After a pause, they have started raising rates again, and it is quite possible that the cost of borrowing will remain elevated for longer, if we listen to what central banks around the world are saying.
The US Federal Reserve, much to President Donald Trump’s annoyance, was unanimous in its decision to raise the Fed fund rate in September. Trump claimed that the rate-setting board was hostile to the idea of lowering interest rates.
But hostility had nothing to do with it. Instead, it was the reality that US inflation could remain higher for longer that prompted the Fed to increase rates. The causes of sticky US inflation can be traced to clumsy policy decisions by Trump.
Meanwhile, Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank (ECB), said that the bank’s decision to raise interest rates in September was a no-brainer. Every ECB policymaker at the meeting agreed that inflation risks were to the upside.
The bank is expected to raise interest rates again before the end of the year, as
inflation
is nearly double its 2 per cent target.
The order of the day
Other central banks that have raised rates include the Bank of Japan, Bank of Korea and Reserve Bank of Australia.
The Reserve Bank of India raised its benchmark policy repo rate for the first time in nearly four years. The hike was driven by rising energy prices, geopolitical pressures and climate change. India’s central bank said that rate cuts are off the table and future decisions will be dependent on inflation data.
Meanwhile, America is hoping that it can reduce energy prices by letting Russia release its diesel, which had been previously blocked by the US. The embarrassing back-pedalling by Trump is unlikely to work.
It is unclear how a temporary reprieve of sanctioned Russia fuel would lower prices, given that available diesel is still in short supply. It merely shifts the problem from one part of the world to another.
It would appear that we are entering a period when central bank monetary tightening could be the order of the day. It seems implausible that the rate of inflation would fall back to many central banks’ preferred target of 2 per cent for a while.
So, we will have to learn to live with interest rates staying higher for longer.
Winners and losers
Not everyone will be unhappy with higher interest rates; some investors might even welcome them.
Savers, for instance, would be delighted if rates stay elevated. They would finally earn higher yields on their savings accounts, money-market accounts and short-term certificates of deposits.
Those close to
retirement
might also appreciate higher interest rates. They can swap their savings for regular, guaranteed income payments for a set number of years.
In some instances, it could even be for the rest of their lives.
When interest rates are low, annuity rates can be abysmally low, too. But when interest rates rise, annuity rates and payouts could go up, regardless of what happens to inflation subsequently.
The reason why central banks are raising interest rates is to quell inflation.
When borrowing rates are high, consumer spending could drop, as indebted households cut back on discretionary spending. It could prompt businesses to delay capital spending and encourage people to save more.
The upshot is that demand for goods and services could drop, which in turn could force businesses to stop raising prices. Interest rates are, admittedly, a blunt tool to address inflation. But it works.
Jam today or tomorrow?
However, rising interest rates can also have an impact on the stock market. In particular, companies whose earnings will materialise only in the distant future could find themselves disproportionately affected. Their future profit when discounted to the present day could be worth less when interest rates are high.
That does not bode well for some businesses that are directly involved in artificial intelligence, where it can be more a case of a promise of jam tomorrow rather than jam today.
But for those businesses that can deliver large dollops of jam today, higher interest rates could be less of a problem.
Banks, for instance, could benefit as their net interest margins widen, thanks to higher rates. They might have to pay more interest to savers; but they can charge even more interest to borrowers, which would increase their net interest income.
Insurance companies could benefit, too. They could earn more from their investments in fixed-income assets such as bonds and government securities.
It is quite possible that stock markets on the whole could react badly to higher interest rates. But provided we own a well-diversified portfolio of assets, it could be a good opportunity to buy more of what we like at better prices.
For me, it couldn’t be easier. As an income investor, I can buy more at today’s more-attractive prices for tomorrow’s dividends.
If the market falls further, will you be ready… or fully invested?

Here’s the thing: three of the four belong to the same family.
Jardine Matheson counts DFI Retail and Hongkong Land among its key operating units.
And all four have
raised their dividends
or payout commitments this year.
Of course, one month of returns says little on its own.
The business underneath tells you more.
Is DFI Retail’s profit growing faster than its sales?
DFI Retail is a pan-Asian retailer with 7,659 outlets across 12 markets.
For context, DFI put out a business update for the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026), so it didn’t disclose revenue, net profit or free cash flow.
Underlying subsidiary sales from continuing businesses rose 4% YoY, while underlying subsidiary profit grew 17%.
In other words, DFI is squeezing more profit out of each sale.
Health & Beauty and Home Furnishings became more profitable, and cost cuts lowered expenses.
DFI also swung to net cash of US$128 million as at 30 September 2026, from net debt of US$22 million three months earlier.
Management raised the bottom of its 2026 underlying profit guidance, which now sits at US$295 million to US$305 million.
It confirmed a 70% payout ratio for 2026 and raised it to 80% for 2027.
DFI is also swapping its Maxim’s stake for Maxim’s Starbucks business in seven Asian markets.
The deal should complete by end-March 2027.
Investors will watch how smoothly DFI absorbs it.
Can Jardine Matheson grow profit while revenue falls?
Jardine Matheson is a diversified, Asia-focused investment company.
Its first-half 2026 (1H2026) numbers look odd.
Revenue fell 7% YoY to US$15.9 billion, yet adjusted underlying profit attributable to shareholders rose 9% to US$735 million.
How did Jardine pull that off?
Higher contributions from Hongkong Land, DFI Retail and Jardine Pacific, plus lower financing costs, more than made up for an 8% drop in Astra’s contribution.
One caveat: US$24 million of Jardine Pacific’s gain came from non-recurring items.
Jardine raised its interim dividend by 8% YoY to US$0.65 per share and now guides for at least US$2.47 per share for the full year.
It also launched a US$500 million share buyback.
The cash picture is less rosy.
Free cash flow fell 23% YoY to US$1.5 billion.
As at 30 June 2026, borrowings of US$14.8 billion exceeded cash of US$7.5 billion.
The planned US$2.4 billion purchase of I-MED Radiology Network will also draw on cash.
Is Hongkong Land’s dividend hike backed by cash?
Hongkong Land owns and manages premium mixed-use property in Asian gateway cities.
Its 1H2026 underlying profit attributable to shareholders rose 11% YoY to US$259.1 million.
Underlying earnings per share rose 14% to US$0.1207 on a smaller share count.
Look closer, and operating profit barely moved.
Most of the gain came from lower net financing charges, which fell to US$56.2 million from US$88 million.
Hongkong Land has now recycled US$3.7 billion of capital, or 93% of its target.
The interim dividend rose by a third to US$0.08 per share.
That’s around 66% of underlying earnings per share.
Free cash flow went the other way – it fell 26% YoY to US$153.2 million as spending on major renovations nearly doubled.
Why does Sembcorp make the list despite falling profit?
Sembcorp Industries
is an energy and urban solutions provider backed by Temasek, a global investment company headquartered in Singapore.
Its 1H2026 revenue climbed 28% YoY to S$3.8 billion on higher energy prices in Singapore and a month’s contribution from Alinta, its newly acquired Australian business.
Profit told a different story.
Net profit attributable to shareholders fell 72% to S$150 million after S$155 million of Alinta transaction costs.
Underlying net profit fell a milder 25% to S$369 million.
Sembcorp still raised its interim dividend by 22% YoY to S$0.11 per share.
Management expects a stronger second half, with help from a new 600MW hydrogen-ready plant, due for completion in 4Q2026, and a full period of Alinta.
Of the four, Sembcorp has the most to prove.
Free cash flow swung to negative S$39 million from positive S$241 million a year ago.
Borrowings rose to S$15.2 billion from S$9 billion at end-2025.
Get Smart: Follow the cash, not just the dividend
A rising dividend is a good sign, but it isn’t the whole story.
Jardine, Hongkong Land and Sembcorp all raised their dividends while free cash flow fell.
DFI didn’t disclose it.
Free cash flow is the lifeblood of dividends.
So when a company you own raises its dividend, check whether cash flow grew alongside it.
If it didn’t, find out whether a one-off spending caused the dip, or whether debt is filling the gap.
One good month won’t tell you that.
The next few sets of results will.

title: US companies slash the least jobs in October in three years
article:
(Nov 5): US employers announced the fewest number of job cuts for any October since 2023, while hiring plans picked up as companies began gearing up for the holiday-shopping season.

 

Companies last month announced 43,994 job cuts, according to data from outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas Inc. That was down 71% from a year earlier, when companies announced the most reductions for any October in more than two decades.

Employers last month also said that they intend to hire nearly 445,000 workers, up 57% from a year ago and the highest for any October since at least 2009, according to Challenger.

The increase was driven entirely by staffing preparations for the busy holiday-shopping period. Amazon Inc, with plans to hire 300,000 workers, accounted for nearly two-thirds of total planned seasonal hiring. United Parcel Service Inc also announced it planned to take on 100,000 workers, according to the report.

At the same time, Challenger noted that the timing of seasonal hiring announcements has shifted to October rather than in September. Temporary holiday staffing has also become more concentrated, with only five companies having announced seasonal hiring plans this year compared to 11 in 2025.

“Seasonal employers are staggering their announcements and waiting longer to see how the season shakes out before they commit to numbers,” Andy Challenger, the company’s chief revenue officer, said in a statement. “They are not cutting deeply, but they are not committing to permanent headcount, either. Seasonal roles give companies the capacity they need for the holidays with an end date built in.”

The data on job cuts and hiring plans underscore a labour market with few layoffs but also limited employment opportunities. The government’s October jobs report on Friday is expected to show a 65,000 increase in payrolls and an unemployment rate holding at 4.2%.

See also: US Treasury borrows record US$839 bil in single week

The top reason employers used when announcing job cuts last month was market and economic conditions, which has overtaken artificial intelligence as the main reason for workforce reductions this year. Recent employment data shows some employers have remained cautious about expanding headcount amid high costs.

title: Pound strength highest since Brexit vote ahead of BOE hike
article:
(Nov 5): A gauge of pound strength rose to its highest level since 2016, supported by resilient UK economic data and expectations for interest-rate hikes.

The Bank of England’s (BOE) pound effective exchange-rate index has been in a steady uptrend since September and this week rose above its May 2025 peak, reaching the strongest level since the Brexit referendum.

UK growth has remained resilient, the labour market has shown signs of stabilising and political risks have eased, helping support the currency. Sterling has outperformed most of its Group-of-10 peers this year and surpassed US$1.35 this week to hit its highest level against the dollar since mid-September.

Attention now turns to the BOE’s policy decision later on Thursday. Markets are pricing a quarter-point rate increase, the first in three years, and traders will focus on guidance for the path ahead. Swaps imply at least two additional increases over the next year, though the recent decline in oil prices may reduce pressure on policymakers to tighten more aggressively.

UK assets have also been supported by Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey’s budget, which contained no major fiscal surprises and was well received by investors. Meanwhile, October data showed Britain’s private sector expanded at the fastest pace in eight months, while a two-year downturn in employment came to an end.

See also: Franc, yen emerge as FX winners as US midterms weaken dollar

The BOE’s index is a measure of the overall change in the trade-weighted exchange value of sterling, and is designed to measure changes in the price competitiveness of traded goods and services.

title: Commerzbank flags deposit competition before UniCredit deal
article:
(Nov 5): Commerzbank AG lowered its outlook for lending income this year amid increasing competition for client money, in one of the last quarters before the lender will be taken over by UniCredit SpA.

Deposits volumes in the German retail unit declined by about €3 billion over the three months through September as Commerzbank decided not to match what it called “exceptionally high offers for new money” by competitors, according to a statement on Thursday.

As a result, the company lowered its outlook for net interest income this year to €8.5 billion from €8.6 billion, while confirming its overall targets for profit and revenue. Net income in the third quarter rose 45% from a year earlier.

“We have seen quite aggressive offerings” of rivals, chief executive officer Bettina Orlopp said in an interview on Bloomberg TV, adding that the drop in deposits wasn’t related to the pending change of control. “We explicitly decided that we would not participate in such an product, and that we would rather accept some outflow for the sake of profitability.”

Orlopp has boosted profitability and shareholders payouts since taking over two years ago, in an ultimately unsuccessful effort to stay independent. After securing close to 50% of the German rival’s shares, UniCredit is expected to effectively take control of Commerzbank in the coming months, in one of the largest bank acquisitions in decades. CEO Andrea Orcel has indicated he will then seek to replace Orlopp and chairman Jens Weidmann.

Third-quarter “trends were disappointing,” RBC analyst Anke Reingen wrote in a note to clients.

See also: Eurozone wage growth to slow sharply next year in boost for ECB

Shares of Commerzbank fell 2.2% at 9.45am in Frankfurt, paring gains this year to just under 8%. They have more than doubled in value under Orlopp.

Commerzbank executives said on a call that they expect deposits to increase again by the end of the fourth quarter, and that they’re comfortable with analysts’ expectations for higher net interest income next year. Provisions for loan losses this year will likely come in slightly below the bank’s target, Orlopp said.

See also: Lagarde to leave ECB early, igniting race to replace her

Orlopp said working group discussions with UniCredit about the pending change of control are “very constructive, and everybody is working towards the objective to to get that done in the right way”.

She also highlighted potential benefits from the tie-up through joint procurement, leveraging each others’ international network, and joint usage of product platforms.

Orcel has outlined plans to cut large parts of Commerzbank’s international network and eliminate as many as 7,000 job cuts in Germany. The German government, which owns almost 13% of Commerzbank, has said it wants to preserve the lender’s important role in funding the national economy.

title: China blocks SoftBank’s US$5.4 bil takeover of ABB robotics unit
article:
(Nov 5): China has blocked the sale of ABB Ltd’s robotics unit to SoftBank Group Corp, dealing a blow to the Japanese investment firm’s plans to expand into physical artificial intelligence (AI).

A Chinese government agency blocked the US$5.4 billion ($6.9 billion) deal, ABB said in an emailed statement. The takeover was widely expected to bolster SoftBank’s revenue and profit while it awaited a boost from OpenAI’s public debut.

SoftBank’s shares were down around 7% in Tokyo on Thursday. A company spokesperson declined to comment.

ABB shares fell as much as 2.2% in early trading in Zurich. The stock was up by nearly a fifth through Wednesday’s close.

The expected proceeds were long expected to be deployed by ABB in other deals. The news cuts ABB’s firepower in half to about US$5 billion, according to Citigroup analyst Martin Wilkie.

Founder Masayoshi Son had listed the deal as a key part of his ambition to play a larger role in the AI build-out. The Tokyo-based firm was looking to take over a business from Swiss-Swedish conglomerate ABB with more than 7,000 employees, which supplies robotic arms and industrial machinery to manufacturers like BMW AG and has a large presence in China.

See also: Marvell reaches US$115 bil deal for Lumentum

Investors worry about Son’s commitments to AI, from SoftBank’s near-US$65 billion bet on OpenAI to pledges of hundreds of billions of dollars on data centre projects. Some had looked to ABB’s expected contribution to SoftBank’s bottom line for assurance that the company was not overextending itself.

“ABB Robotics lacks the cutting-edge innovation found across SoftBank’s physical AI start-up portfolio, but its domain expertise and manufacturing know-how had been expected to transform robotic concepts into actual businesses,” said Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Kirk Boodry.

Beijing’s move against the ABB deal casts more uncertainty over SoftBank’s ambitions, and reflects the Chinese government’s renewed emphasis on safeguarding its data and technology in the AI era.

See also: Ray-Ban heir proposes family buyout after €31 bil Czech bid

In April, China’s powerful National Development and Reform Commission blocked Meta Platforms Inc’s US$2 billion acquisition of agentic AI start-up Manus, issuing a one-line notice saying it had decided to prohibit foreign investment in the start-up in accordance with laws and regulations.

SoftBank’s acquisition was similarly subjected to a foreign investment security review by the state planner, according to an earlier report in the Financial Times. China’s Office of the Working Mechanism for Foreign Investment Security Review prohibited the deal, according to the ABB statement.

Beijing, recognizing how data is the foundation of AI, has this year clamped down on the transfer of vital information abroad. That’s true also of the robotics arena, where data is fundamental to eventually making robots work.

Japan is home to many of the world’s biggest industrial robot makers including Fanuc Corp, Yaskawa Electric Corp and Kawasaki Heavy Industries Ltd. Most have partnered with Nvidia Corp to explore ways to use AI inside factories, hospitals and logistics networks and stay ahead of rising competition from China.

title: Micron said to pause work on US$4.5 bil Taiwan plant after labour spat
article:
(Nov 5): Micron Technology Inc has suspended plans for a memory chip plant in Taiwan due to a protracted labour dispute, according to people familiar with the matter, throwing into question the fate of a major production base for crucial artificial intelligence (AI) components.

The US company has all but halted construction of a plant in the northern Taiwanese city of Taoyuan, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the deliberations are private. Executives are concerned about mounting uncertainties, including the risk that an agreement with a local labour union will get overturned. Micron has informed Taiwanese officials and a supplier about its plans to suspend construction in the city, the people said.

Tensions between Micron and its workers flared this year after employees demanded higher compensation, seeking more of the record profits generated from the AI build-out. The potential disruption to Micron’s plans in Taiwan — an island that produces three-fifths of the US firm’s conventional chips — threatens to further cloud a market already grappling with endemic shortages of memory.

Micron — which has invested close to US$50 billion ($63.8 billion) in Taiwan over three decades — had planned on making high-bandwidth memory and DRAM at the new Taoyuan plant using top-end equipment from ASML Holding NV. While it isn’t considered a giant facility by modern standards, those components are intertwined with Nvidia Corp accelerators and the global AI data centre boom, and in such short supply that prices are skyrocketing.

“Taiwan plays an important role in Micron’s global footprint, and our operations today continue as normal,” Micron said in a statement, without addressing questions about the Taoyuan complex. “We are confident in maintaining business continuity for our customers.”

Micron secured a deal with the bigger of its two unions in October, but the company may need to renegotiate because some employees are balking at the terms, according to the people.

See also: Nvidia partner Foxconn sales up 46% on AI demand

The suspension raises the possibility Micron will reconsider plans for its broader manufacturing hub in Taiwan, which helps it compete with South Korea’s Samsung Electronics Co and SK Hynix Inc, and China’s CXMT Corp.

Micron had budgeted US$3 billion to US$4.5 billion towards the Taoyuan complex, which included purchases of ASML gear, one of the people said. There’s still some minor work being done on the site to ensure its safety, but construction will freeze after that, the people added. Dubbed Fab 11E, it was previously scheduled to come online in 2028.

Micron is Taiwan’s largest foreign investor, and it would be a major blow to the island if the company scaled back there.

See also: DayOne secures US$237 mil loan for Hong Kong data centre

Taiwan’s economy and stock market have gotten a boost from the AI boom, with the likes of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC) building plants at an unprecedented pace. Yet its viability as a long-term investment destination is at risk from potential Chinese military intervention.

Even as Micron considers slowing down in Taiwan, it’s racing to ready factories elsewhere. It’s committed to investing US$250 billion in US manufacturing, including in New York state. It has also been expanding in Japan and Singapore.

Taiwan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs didn’t comment on Micron’s move to pause some expansion, but said the government was helping the company implement investment plans.

“The government supports the legal agreement the company has reached with the union, and will shoulder and share responsibilities with the local government to help resolve the differences and create a win-win outcome,” the ministry said in a statement to Bloomberg News. The Taoyuan government said it hasn’t been notified of a suspension, though it’s hoping Micron and its employees can reach a consensus.

The Taoyuan plant isn’t the largest for Micron in Taiwan. But it’s a showpiece project for a US company with an outsized local presence.

Taiwan currently accounts for 60% of Micron’s global output of DRAM or dynamic random access chips, the common form of memory used in computers and phones. The area also produces a big chunk of its high-bandwidth memory or HBM, which is used in AI systems.

The island is Micron’s largest site in terms of personnel, with 15,000 employees or about a quarter of the company’s total. The Taoyuan union represents fewer than 3,000, with the bulk of the remainder joining the far larger Taichung body.

The Taoyuan group has demanded Micron distribute 15% of its operating profit to global employees, because Samsung and SK Hynix have adopted similar measures. Union chair Jerry Lin said the employees also want all-cash incentives, rather than partially in stock.

The union is now trying to form a bigger group by recruiting members from the Taichung body — to help try and annul the existing pact. It will then demand Micron restart negotiations, Lin said.

While Micron hasn’t disclosed terms of the standing deal, Taiwan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs said the agreement would lift junior engineers’ annual packages by more than two-fold to NT$4 million (US$121,450 or $155,045), on average. Senior engineers would get a three-fold bump to NT$6 million. The mean annual pay for an engineer at listed local semiconductor firms was NT$2.58 million in 2025, according to employment site 104 Job Bank.

Micron felt confident the agreement reached with the larger union was legally binding, according to a person familiar with the matter. Taichung union chair Mark Hsu also acknowledged its legality, but said he respected the move by its smaller peer to form a bigger organisation.

Talks with the Taoyuan union are ongoing. “We look forward to reaching an agreement,” Micron said.

title: ArcelorMittal jumps on profit boost from tougher steel curbs
article:
(Nov 5): ArcelorMittal SA’s shares jumped more than 6% as earnings beat expectations, offering an early sign that new trade curbs on European imports are boosting profitability.

The biggest steelmaker outside China brought in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation of US$2.02 billion in the third quarter (3Q), beating an US$1.89 billion estimate of analysts surveyed by Bloomberg. Earnings stood at US$2.06 billion in the previous quarter.

It’s the first set of results since a significant tightening of EU steel-import restrictions took effect on July 1, with the measures cutting tariff-free import quotas and doubling the duty on other shipments to 50%. The bloc’s carbon levy on imports will also help shield its steelmakers.

The restrictions have raised expectations that European producers will regain pricing power as cheaper imports become harder to bring into the region, which accounts for about half of ArcelorMittal’s steel sales.

When India, the US and Latin American economies raised protectionist barriers to combat a wave of Chinese exports, there were fears that the European market would be flooded with cheap steel. The levy hikes have soothed those concerns, while Beijing is also slowly moving to target overcapacity in its near one-billion-tonne a year steel sector.

See also: Air Liquide’s sales grow on sustained AI-related demand

ArcelorMittal has also been bringing capacity back online to capture more of the European market, including blast-furnace restarts in France, Poland and Spain. Still, analysts at UBS Group AG have cautioned that the benefits from Europe’s tighter trade regime may take time to show up fully in producer earnings.

An “encouraging development is the support we are seeing from European policy,” ArcelorMittal chief executive Aditya Mittal said in a statement on Thursday. The measures support “higher capacity utilization and profitability over time,” he added.

Higher energy costs in the fuel-intensive sector were a headwind over the quarter, Mittal said, adding that this was being increasingly offset by higher steel pricing in Europe.

See also: Ports giant DP World redraws Hormuz logistics with truck bet

ArcelorMittal also idled its Kryvyi Rih operations in Ukraine during 3Q after a series of missile strikes damaged the site and killed workers. The shutdown resulted in US$852 million of impairment charges and US$293 million of exceptional charges in the quarter, the company said.

ArcelorMittal rallied as much as 6.6% to €58.78 a share, in the biggest gain since July.

title: China's crackdown pushes wealthy to gold, lifting Hong Kong jewellery sales
article:
(Nov 5): Hong Kong’s jewellery and watch sales have surged to their highest level since 2019 despite China’s broader luxury slowdown, as the rich turn to gold and gemstones to preserve wealth amid Beijing’s tightening grip over their offshore investments.

Sales of jewellery, watches, clocks and valuable gifts jumped 22% year-on-year to HK$45.8 billion (US$5.8 billion or $7.5 billion) in the first nine months, far outpacing overall retail growth, according to latest government data. The sector accounted for about 15% of Hong Kong’s total retail sales.

Hong Kong jewellery sales maintained double-digit growth in the latest quarter even as luxury spending plunged over 10% in mainland China, as Beijing intensified its tax scrutiny of wealthy residents’ overseas assets. That’s helped soften the blow for global giants from Hermès International SCA to Cie Financiere Richemont SA, which generate substantial sales from the Asia-Pacific region.

The shopping spree in Hong Kong underscores how Chinese consumers are now prioritising wealth preservation over growth. Gold and precious stones have emerged as rare safe havens, as Beijing’s crackdown on capital outflows has made it harder for mainland residents to use traditional channels to invest and park wealth overseas, while physical gold is widely viewed as a reliable store of value and is less vulnerable to regulatory shifts.

Meanwhile, a strong yuan and Hong Kong’s tax-free status have added to the city’s appeal to Chinese shoppers, contributing to a strong tourism recovery.

Adding to the pressure, last year’s AI-driven stock market rally has soured, while a protracted property downturn continues to trap a large share of household savings.

See also: China boosts market defence with National Team, buybacks

“People have a surging interest in pursuing certainties, as they are concerned about the recent tax policy changes,” said Manna Wang, an insurance sales agent in Hong Kong. “They want to be 100% sure that their wealth won’t change drastically in the future. High returns are no longer the priority.”

Over the past several months, authorities in Beijing have restricted mainland firms from listing in Hong Kong, tightened controls on offshore stock trading and ramped up scrutiny of foreign trusts and insurance products.

See also: China plans broad AI guardrails after global security lapses

While Wang’s mainland Chinese clients used to consult her on high-return insurance policies, they are now asking her to take them shopping for gold jewellery. They are also switching to fixed-income insurance products that come with lower returns but carry fewer tax obligations, Wang said.

Wang’s clients spent as much as US$15,000 per person buying gold from jewellers including China’s Laopu Gold Co — one of their favourite destinations, she said. The main draw is a strong yuan, making exchange rates more favourable, as well as Hong Kong’s tax-free status, Wang said. As a result, jewellery prices in the city could be more than 5% lower than in the mainland, she added.

Jewellery has become a bright spot for global luxury brands, while sales of clothes and handbags disappointed due to sluggish demand in China. LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE reported an 8% organic growth in the sector in the first nine months, the fastest among all divisions. At Kering SA, jewellery sales jumped 17% during the same period, compared with a 2% decline in fashion and leather goods.

Shares of Hong Kong-listed jewellers jumped on Thursday, tracking a rally in gold prices after the US midterm elections. Laopu shares rose more than 8%, the most in almost three months, and Luk Fook Holdings International Ltd's stock gained 5%.

Part of the reason for the surge in jewellery sales is the rise in gold prices, which climbed to a record high earlier this year. That rally has boosted the value of gold jewellery, said Alexis Bonhomme, the chief executive officer of luxury consultancy Trinity Asia.

Sales growth in Hong Kong has remained strong even as gold prices have retreated in recent months, indicating demand is resilient.

A sustained tourism rebound is helping drive the retail surge. Visitor arrivals rose 12% in the first nine months with the majority from mainland China. That’s returned to 87% of the level in 2018 before the city became battered by years of political turmoil and Covid closure, marking the strongest post-pandemic recovery yet.
